items.headline: Rockwood Rocket Tone: 6-Time All-Canadian, and “an Absolute Disaster” as a Sire
items.post_text:
Rockwood Rocket Tone was named All-Canadian six times running. Senior yearling, two-year-old, three-year-old, aged bull. Only two animals in Holstein history ever beat that run.

This was 1949 and the years after, when bull classes still filled the coliseum at the Royal Winter Fair. A champion male could stop traffic on looks alone.

Then his daughters freshened.

E.Y. Morwick, one of the sharpest historians of the breed, needed six words. "A dud, just an absolute disaster." Not as a show bull. As a transmitter.

Andrew Hunt tells the full story in The Bullvine this week, with one number worth keeping. Of the champion bulls of that era, roughly one in six could actually breed.

Those bull classes have since disappeared from the big fairs. The males moved to the sеmen catalogs.

The stage changed. The problem did not. We still weigh what we can see above what we can measure, and the result still lands a season later, on the farm.

When you pick a sire, which of the two is doing more of the work?

#sеmen #cattlebreeding #dairygenetics #holstein

items.headline: Start Where It Hurts: How to Implement Dairy Technology That Scales
items.post_text:
One dairy milked 4,500 cows on two rotary platforms. Its breeding team was ten people per milking.

After installing automated sorting gates, that number dropped to two. Eight people moved to higher-value work. The herd did not shrink. The labor bill did.

Progressive Dairy laid out how this actually happens this week, and the mechanics are worth reading. Sort gates route cows by rule, not by memory. Every cow between 95 and 120 days in milk goes to the hoof trimmer each Wednesday, automatically. Breeding cows and treatment cows separate in a single pass.

The piece makes a quieter point too. The farms that win with technology do not start big. They name their most expensive problem first, missed heats or slow milking or the labor crunch, and solve only that. Then they add one piece at a time, on the same cow IDs.

Most technology is bought before the problem is named. That is the step everyone skips.

What is the one problem you would automate first?

#dairyfarming #precisionlivestock #herdmanagement #agritech

items.headline: Many growers still find ‘no meaningful benefit’ from AI use on the farm: survey
items.post_text:
Purdue asked 400 farmers about AI on their operations. More than half, 52%, said the tools provide no meaningful benefit right now.

The detail underneath is sharper than the headline. Agtech usually sells AI as a labor saver. Only 14% of these farmers expected it to cut labor needs or cost. A slightly larger group, 22.8%, thought it would lift production.

Jennifer Marston, writing in AgFunderNews this week, quotes the barometer's lead economist Michael Langemeier. His read is plain. Most respondents simply have not figured out how these tools help their operation yet.

He points to what he calls facts on the ground. A tool can tell you to plant corn on a given day. Weather or a broken machine can make that day impossible.

That last point is the whole story. The barrier is rarely belief in the technology. It is whether the technology survives the conditions of a real working day.

What would it take for a tool to earn a permanent place on your operation?

#agritech #livestock #precisionag #farmtech

items.headline: Holstein’s 60-Inch Rule: Why Breeders Are Backing It With 53%-vs-21% Math
items.summary: Two weeks after the May 2026 stature penalty, breeders answered back with heritability math: 53% vs 21%.
items.post_text:
Two weeks after Holstein USA's new stature penalty landed, docking cows over 60 inches, the sharpest response wasn't outrage. It was a heritability lesson. Andrew Hunt, writing in The Bullvine this week, traces how one comment reframed the debate.

Quebec breeder Emeric Lebacle made the point almost in passing: stature runs about 53% heritable by Lactanet's numbers, while feet and legs sit around 21% for the major score. Push hard on a low-heritability trait and progress crawls. Stature responds roughly 2.5 times more reliably to selection.

The penalty bites gradually: no deduction at 60 inches, minus 0.15 at 61, climbing to minus 3.45 at 70. Taller cows tend to exit the herd earlier, and an early cull costs roughly $2,000 per replacement heifer.

Feet and legs stay weak even in today's top GTPI bulls, and the penalty doesn't fix that directly. A short cow once denied an "Excellent" score became one of Wisconsin's highest lifetime milk producers.

Where would you draw the line between structural durability and chasing a number on paper?

#genetics #Holstein #dairybreeding #heritability #cattlegenetics

items.headline: Increase breeding results with synch protocols and estrus detection aids
items.summary: Latest synchronization protocols and estrus detection aids for greater reproductive success.
items.post_text:
Half or more of your cows can be noncycling when a synch protocol starts.

That number comes from Jordan Thomas, writing in Progressive Cattle this week, and it gets worse after a long calving season. A synchronized cow that never shows heat is a wasted shot.

The Beef Reproduction Task Force publishes validated protocol sheets every year. For heifers not yet cycling, longer progestin protocols like the 14-day CIDR-prostaglandin give more time to reach puberty. For cows, the classic is 7-day Cosynch plus CIDR, with a newer 7 & 7 Synch variant adding an extra prostaglandin dose.

Breeding indicator patches add a decision layer on top. If 50% or more of the patch ink rubs off, that female is a strong candidate for sexed sеmen. Less than half, and conventional sеmen may be safer.

So much of this rides on what happens before insemination. Detection is what tells you whether the protocol worked at all.

Are estrus detection aids underused on your operation, or already standard?

#reproduction #cattlebreeding #ArtificialInsemination #sеmen #dairygenetics

items.headline: Your Oldest Cow Isn't a Cull — She's a $3,000 Heifer You Don't Have to Buy
items.summary: Replacement heifer costs hit $3,010/head, up 164% since 2019, making cow longevity an economic strategy; reproductive health (clearing uterine infections) is one of four pillars keeping cows productive longer.
items.post_text:
Keeping cows one extra lactation saves a 200-cow dairy about $60,000 a year.

That is the math Andrew Hunt lays out in The Bullvine this week, and it starts with what a replacement costs. A dairy heifer now runs $3,010, up from $1,140 in April 2019. Top auction prices in California and Minnesota have crossed $4,000.

The national average is 2.7 lactations. Move it to 3.7 and that herd raises roughly 20 fewer heifers a year. Buying your way out is getting harder. USDA counted 3.914 million replacement heifers this January, the lowest since 1978.

Hunt names four pillars behind the extra lactation: transition nutrition, udder health, foot care, and reproductive health, specifically clearing uterine infections across consecutive cycles.

The ceiling is higher than most herds imagine. Gillette Emperor Smurf EX-91, a Holstein in her 18th lactation, has produced 478,163 pounds of milk, a Guinness World Record.

The fourth pillar is where fertility work quietly pays for itself.

What's the oldest cow still earning her keep in your herd, and what's actually keeping her there?

#reproduction #dairyfarming #cattlebreeding #cowlongevity #dairyeconomics

items.headline: Does delaying conception improve profitability?
items.summary: Study on dry period length and days open: intermediate-length dry periods gave higher milk production and better fertility; questions whether delaying conception in high-producing modern Holsteins improves profitability.
items.post_text:
Delaying conception does not pay off, not even in the highest-producing herds.

That is the finding from a retrospective study by Overton and Eicker covering more than 109,000 Holstein cows across 60 US dairy herds, reported this week by Alvaro Garcia in Progressive Dairy.

The question was reasonable. Modern Holsteins hold their lactation curve longer than cows a generation ago, so some producers wondered whether longer days open would mean more milk before pregnancy took its toll.

The data said otherwise. Longer days open in one lactation raised replacement risk in the next. Dry period length followed a curve, not a line: both too short and too long raised early-removal risk, with roughly 60 days best. Cows that conceived earlier and kept a traditional dry period made more milk through 90 days and got pregnant sooner next lactation.

Garcia's conclusion is that reproductive efficiency is not a pregnancy checkbox. It is a long-term driver of survivability and profit.

Where is your herd's dry period landing, and does it match what the cow's transition needs?

#dairy #reproduction #cattle #fertility #herdhealth

items.headline: New technology, new possibilities: How to introduce artificial intelligence into your dairy
items.summary: CATTLEytics founder Shari van de Pol explains how AI helps producers with data analytics, breeding schedules, nutrition, disease diagnosis and employee management on dairies of any size.
items.post_text:
The dairy AI problem is not collecting data but acting on it, and the fix starts with one question, not the whole farm.

That is Shari van de Pol, a computer engineer turned large-animal vet, on the Progressive Dairy Podcast in a piece by Patryce Eldredge LeFevre this week. "You can have all the information in the world, but if you're not actually making any changes, what's the point?"

Van de Pol founded CATTLEytics around exactly that gap. Her method is unglamorous. Open ChatGPT, Copilot or Perplexity. Ask a real question about your operation. If the answer feels off, push back and ask it to refine.

She is clear about the limits. AI does not replace the nutritionist or the vet. It fills gaps and spots patterns across feed, breeding and health records. She also sees it as a leveler, giving smaller operations analysis only large dairies could afford.

The tool is only as useful as the question you bring it.

What is the one recurring decision you would hand to AI first?

#dairy #AI #agtech #dataanalytics #cattle

items.headline: Orbem begins US rollout of MRI-based in-ovo sexing tech
items.summary: German startup Orbem, backed by 55.5M euro Series B, deploys MRI+AI system determining chick sex in-ovo with 99.5% accuracy in under a second; first US hatchery system live, second in mid-August; in-ovo sexing already covers 40% of EU commercial layer flock.
items.post_text:
An MRI scanner can now sex a chick inside the egg with 99.5% accuracy, in under a second.

Orbem's system is running at its first US hatchery, according to AgFunderNews this week. The Munich-founded startup, with a Texas office since 2025, calls it "Genus Focus": an MRI scanner paired with AI that identifies a chick's developing reproductive organs around day 11 to 12 of incubation.

A second US installation is scheduled for mid-August, a third for 2027. Jennifer Volz, the company's head of global business development, says a major US retailer will announce its own rollout soon.

Europe got there first. In-ovo sexing already covers 40% of the EU's commercial layer flock, and more than 281 million female chicks have been selected this way since 2021. Orbem runs the system as pay-per-use rather than selling hardware, and reports being profitable after a 55.5 million euro Series B in January.

Sex determination before birth, at near-perfect accuracy, keeps showing up as the economics driver across species. Where else in animal agriculture is this precision still missing?

#agritech #genetics #AI #innovation #poultry

items.headline: Creating pregnancies in the heat with Ben Dickman
items.summary: Podcast transcript: Arizona dairy Dickman and Sons raised its summer 21-day pregnancy rate from the low teens to about 20% after a four-year cooling system investment, using CowManager activity monitoring, an 80-day voluntary waiting period, sexed and beef semen, and genomic culling.
items.post_text:
An Arizona dairy pushed its summer pregnancy rate from the low teens to roughly 20%, and the cooling starts in March.

Ben Dickman, third-generation owner of Dickman and Sons Dairy in Coolidge, told Progressive Dairy editor Matti McBride the farm hit 105°F that early this year. Nights still run from the high 90s into triple digits.

The 3,600-cow dairy uses exit lane drenches, flip fans and manger drenchers tied to humidity, dew point and wind. Four years in, it paid for itself in a year and a half, not the projected three.

Reproduction runs on an 80-day voluntary waiting period and CowManager monitoring, aiming to get sеmen into every cow by 99 days in milk. Genomics decide who stays: low scorers get culled, sexed sеmen goes to heifers, beef sеmen to second-lactation-plus cows, and the bottom 20% is sold twice a year.

Most heat-stress conversations focus on the animal in the moment. Dickman's numbers point to an infrastructure bet made years before the heat arrived.

What payback horizon does your dairy budget for cooling investments?

#dairyreproduction #hеatstress #cattlebreeding #genomics #dairyfarming

items.headline: Exclusive: Calysta hires new CEO, seeks new capital as JV partner ends financial support
items.summary: Gas fermentation firm Calysta brought in new CEO Berend Jan Kingma after its China JV partner Adisseo ended financial support and halted production at the Chongqing single-cell protein plant; Calysseo 2025 unaudited results show $78.7M assets, $63.9M liabilities, $710k revenue and a $15.5M net loss.
items.post_text:
A single-cell protein plant that booked $710,000 in revenue and a $15.5 million loss has stopped production.

It belongs to Calysseo, the joint venture between gas-fermentation company Calysta and animal nutrition group Adisseo, in Chongqing, China. Elaine Watson, writing in AgFunderNews, reported that Adisseo told the Shanghai Stock Exchange on June 18 it would not renew a loan to the venture after a failed bid for outside financing, citing a "severe shortage of working capital."

Adisseo warned the plant needed "substantial and sustainable financial support" to resume upgrades. Calysseo's unaudited 2025 numbers: $78.7 million in assets, $63.9 million in liabilities.

Calysta has a new CEO, Berend Jan Kingma, formerly of InspiraFarms, FirstWave Group and Miro Forestry. Cofounder Alan Shaw, now non-executive chair, told AgFunderNews the focus is "debottlenecking downstream processing" to raise the capital the plant needs.

Turning methane into feed protein for aquaculture and petfood was a capital-intensive bet. This is what it costs to learn whether the science scales before the money runs out.

Does the science need more time, or more money?

#agritechdeals #alternativeprotein #feedtech #agtechfunding #startups

items.headline: Key performance areas to focus on with automated milking systems
items.post_text:
A robotic milking herd's ideal average is 145 to 160 days in milk, and only strong breeding keeps it there.

Jason French, Commercial Portfolio Manager at DeLaval North America, laid out the math in Progressive Dairy this week.

Automated milking performance splits into two sides. On the cow side, producers set traffic rules: cows in their first 100 days of lactation get more robot visits, cows nearing dry-off get fewer. Hitting that 145 to 160 day window needs strong reproductive performance behind it.

Activity monitors and progesterone testing feed that side, sharpening heat detection and breeding accuracy so fresh cows keep entering the herd on schedule.

On the robot side, French sets his own bar: incomplete milkings should stay in the low single digits, and higher peak milk flow should keep box time short, since box time caps how many cows a robot handles daily.

The two dashboards rarely get read together, though they track the same herd.

Which one gets checked more often on your farm, the cow numbers or the robot numbers?

#dairyfarming #automatedmilking #reproduction #precisionlivestock #dairytech
items.author: Jason French

items.headline: New genetic tools could match bulls to your farm's environment
items.summary: University of Tennessee beef specialist Troy Rowan and land-grant researchers, with the American Angus Association, are developing genetic-by-environment (GxE) tools and adaptive indicator traits like hair shedding scores, aiming to rebuild EPDs with satellite climate data so bull genetics match local heat and forage conditions instead of an assumed average.
items.post_text:
A top bull's genetics do not perform the same in Florida and in Montana, and most breeding tools still assume they do.

Raney Rapp writes about this in Farm Progress this week. Researchers are studying genetic by environment interaction, or GxE: the idea that a sire's genetic value shifts with climate and management.

University of Tennessee beef specialist Troy Rowan put it plainly. Average environments don't exist and average management doesn't exist.

Artificial insemination made elite genetics available everywhere. It also erased traits that helped cattle handle heat or poor forage at home. One early fix already works: hair shedding scores that gauge heat and fescue tolerance.

Land grant universities and the American Angus Association are going further. They are rebuilding expected progeny differences, the scorecards breeders use to pick sires. The new versions will add satellite climate data and real farm records.

Selection tools are moving past breed and carcass numbers, toward genetics matched to the farm they will actually work on.

Would knowing your bull's GxE profile change which sire you buy next?

#cattlegenetics #beefcattle #EPD #genomics #cattlebreeding
items.author: Raney Rapp

items.headline: The $1,300 Gap Between the Bull You Want and the Bull You Should Buy
items.summary: Bullvine analysis of Canada's 20 most-used Holstein sires found some rank 96th percentile for overall LPI but only 31st for Health & Welfare, which is just 8% of the index; Lactanet Pro$ data and a US DWP$ validation put the gap at roughly $1,300 in lifetime profit per daughter, driven by differences in lameness and mastitis rates.
items.post_text:
A 96th-percentile LPI bull can rank 31st for health, a $1,300 gap per daughter.

Murray Hunt writes about it in The Bullvine this week. LPI is Lactanet's genetic merit index for Holstein sires in Canada. Hunt checked the country's 20 most-used sires against its six new subindexes. Some bulls sat at the 96th percentile overall but ranked only 31st for Health and Welfare.

Health and Welfare carries 8% of the total score, next to Production at 40% and Longevity and Type at 32%. Top-quartile sires for health keep 7.4% more daughters at six years, worth $1,300 more per daughter. Their daughters show 15.9 points less lameness and 14.9 points less mastitis.

Hunt calls the composite score a flattering headshot: one number, easy to post and sell. He says the subindexes are the scan that shows where the joint is failing.

A composite score is built to average. Averaging is what hides the one weak trait that costs the most later.

How many of your last sire purchases would survive a look at their subindexes alone?

#Holstein #dairygenetics #cattlebreeding #geneticselection #Lactanet
items.author: Murray Hunt

items.headline: Improving human-animal relationship in cattle production
items.summary: University of Calgary researcher Maria Camila Ceballos links fear-based cattle handling to lower reproductive performance and pregnancy rates; a survey of 100+ western Canada cow-calf handlers and a separate Brazil study found trained stockpeople kept calmer, more consistent handling through a full workday, while untrained ones grew rougher over time; four training formats tested showed no clear winner.
items.post_text:
Cows that fear their handlers get pregnant less often.

Maria Camila Ceballos, writing in Progressive Dairy this week, lays out the mechanism. Fear from handling, not just illness or nutrition, lowers reproductive performance, milk yield and growth. In beef cattle specifically, higher fear responses tracked with lower pregnancy rates.

Her University of Calgary team surveyed more than 100 western Canada cow-calf handlers and ran a separate study in Brazil comparing trained and untrained stockpeople. Trained handlers kept calm, consistent behavior through an entire workday. Untrained ones got rougher as the day wore on, with more shouting, more prods, more accidents.

The team tested four training formats: in-person with demonstrations, in-person without, hybrid, and fully online. None stood out. The researchers suspect the problem isn't format but inconsistent content and delivery across training programs.

Fertility work usually starts at the chute or the sync protocol. This research says it starts earlier, at how the handler walks up to the cow.

Does your team's handling style get measured the same way as your conception rate?

#reproduction #cattlewelfare #dairyfarming #beefcattle #stockmanship
items.author: Maria Camila Ceballos

items.headline: Mycotoxins: A potential hidden threat to reproductive efficiency
items.summary: Studies show that mycotoxin exposure can directly lead to reproductive problems detected at preg checking, including delayed maturation of oocytes, damage to genetic material and reduced ovarian function; zearalenone, aflatoxins, DOM-1 and T-2 toxin each impair fertility in cows and bulls through distinct mechanisms, and standard feed tests miss chronic low-level exposure.
items.post_text:
Mycotoxins in feed can alter 345 genes in a calf embryo, and they are a hidden cause of open cows at preg check.

Cathy Bandyk of Innovad lays out the mechanism in Progressive Cattle this week.

Zearalenone is a mold toxin common in grain, byproducts and forage. It binds to estrogen receptors in the cow. That shows up as abnormal estrus, swollen vulvas and fewer active follicles.

In bulls, zearalenone can lower libido and shrink testicles. High exposure can leave a bull sterile.

Aflatoxin works differently. It attacks sеmen viability and DNA directly. In the study Bandyk cites, 345 genes were altered in aflatoxin-exposed blastocysts.

DOM-1 reduces sperm motility. T-2 toxin causes late-term abortions.

Standard feed tests miss chronic, low-level exposure. Bandyk recommends biomonitoring instead, testing blood directly for mycotoxin residue.

Fertility work usually starts at the sync protocol or the sеmen tank. This research says it can start earlier, in the feed bunk.

If this fall's preg check shows more open or late-bred females than usual, is feed on your list of suspects?

#reproduction #sеmen #cattlefertility #dairygenetics #mycotoxins
items.author: Cathy Bandyk

items.headline: Using genomics to hedge your bet for healthier cattle
items.summary: Igenity veterinarian Kirk Ramsey argues genomic selection extends beyond growth and carcass traits to disease resilience, citing 12-18% heritability for bovine respiratory disease and flagging bovine congestive heart failure as an emerging genetic-risk trait.
items.post_text:
Bovine respiratory disease is 12-18% heritable, so genomic selection can lower a herd's disease risk before a vaccine is ever needed.

Kirk Ramsey, a veterinarian with Igenity, writes in Progressive Cattle this week that health responds to genetic selection the same way growth and carcass quality always have.

BRD remains one of the costliest diseases in the beef industry, much of it hidden in subclinical cases nobody treats. That range doesn't decide whether a calf gets sick. It means producers can pick animals with lower predisposition and shift a herd's odds over generations.

The same logic applies to calving ease, fertility, heifer pregnancy rate and stayability. Ramsey also flags bovine congestive heart failure, where genetics appears to shape risk.

The idea traces to a hard calving Ramsey attended as a young vet. The producer watching him work put it plainly: "The only thing that matters in this line of work is a live calf."

Selection decides which animals need less treating to begin with.

Where does disease resilience show up in your own selection criteria?

#genetics #genomics #cattlebreeding #cattlehealth #beefcattle
items.author: Kirk Ramsey

items.headline: Nordic Holstein Coancestry Rose Twentyfold. Your Inbreeding Percentage Won’t Show You.
items.summary: A 2024 Journal of Dairy Science study by Tenhunen et al. (Aarhus University, VikingGenetics) found that while pedigree analysis of Nordic Holstein showed diversity improving, genomic analysis of the same population found female coancestry rising from 0.02% to 0.39% per year through the genomic-selection transition; Nordic Jersey moved the opposite direction.
items.post_text:
Nordic Holstein females are now getting 20 times more related to each other every year, and pedigree records show none of it.

Andrew Hunt writes about it in The Bullvine this week. His source is a 2024 Journal of Dairy Science paper by Tenhunen and colleagues at Aarhus University and VikingGenetics. They studied one Nordic Holstein population two ways. Pedigree analysis said diversity was improving. Genomic analysis looked at the DNA itself. It found the opposite. Female coancestry rose from 0.02% to 0.39% a year through the shift to genomic selection. Nordic Jersey moved the other way.

The gap traces to genomic testing itself. Breeders can now rank a heifer's genetic merit at birth. The same top-scoring heifers then become repeat donors for flushing and embryo production. VikingGenetics material shows about 10,000 female tests and 4,000 embryos a year.

Two instruments looked at one herd and reached opposite verdicts. The higher-resolution one belongs in every mating decision, not just the annual pedigree report.

Would your next sеmen order change if you saw the genomic number instead of the pedigree one?

#genetics #Holstein #dairybreeding #inbreeding #cattlegenetics
items.author: Andrew Hunt

items.headline: Bring next-generation technology to the parlor you already own
items.summary: GEA dairy equipment specialist Andy Hughes on modernizing an existing milking parlor instead of rebuilding it: a New York dairy milked 500 more cows after adding new front ends and meters, and a farm using semi-automated milking cut eight stalls and one staff position while nearly doubling turns per hour, with a projected three-year payback.
items.post_text:
One dairy needed eight fewer stalls and one less worker after adding semi-automated milking to its existing parlor.

Andy Hughes writes in Progressive Dairy this week about dairies getting more out of the parlor they already have. He walks in asking one question: what is this dairy trying to accomplish.

Semi-automated systems handle teat prep, milk harvest and post-dip inside the unit. They don't replace the parlor itself. One farm using the technology nearly doubled how many cow groups it milks each hour and expects a three-year payback.

Smaller upgrades compound too. A New York dairy added new front ends and meters to its existing parlor and ended up milking 500 more cows. Newer meters also feed cloud dashboards, so a manager can check yesterday's milking data without digging through paper reports.

The industry usually talks about the next parlor to build. This story is about the one already standing in the barn.

What upgrade would unlock the most capacity in your current parlor?

#dairytechnology #dairyfarming #precisionlivestock #automation #milkingequipment
items.author: Andy Hughes

items.headline: Future Breeder Program to build next generation of dairy breeders
items.summary: GenoSource's new Future Breeder Program will award five embryo packages (three embryos each) to youth at World Dairy Expo: three through the showmanship contest (one per age division, drawn from each division's top 10 finalists) and two through the fitting competition (drawn from the top five fitters among males and females).
items.post_text:
GenoSource will give five youth winners at World Dairy Expo real embryo packages this October, not just ribbons.

Patryce Eldredge LeFevre reports on the new Future Breeder Program in Progressive Dairy this week. Five packages, three embryos each, go out at the show.

Three come from the showmanship contest, one per age division, drawn at random from each division's top 10 finalists. Two more come from the fitting competition, drawn from the top five fitters among males and females.

Laura Demmer, GenoSource's director of marketing, names the gap the program targets. "The one area we know dairy youth maybe do not have as much control over is the animals they get to take to the show ring." After winning, a young breeder still has to line up recipients and later run genomic tests on the resulting calves.

Skill in the ring has always been visible. Access to elite genetics rarely is, and that access shapes who keeps competing at the top.

Which matters more for a young breeder future: the ribbon or the genetics behind the calf they led in?

#dairygenetics #dairybreeding #WorldDairyExpo #agritech #cattlebreeding
items.author: Patryce Eldredge LeFevre

items.headline: Preg check early, cull strategically: Using pregnancy diagnosis to improve herd profitability
items.summary: Kacie McCarthy, a beef cow-calf specialist at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, explains how early pregnancy diagnosis (rectal palpation, ultrasound or blood test, detectable 28 to 45 days after breeding) helps producers predict calving dates and guide culling and replacement decisions, since cows that conceive early stay in the herd longer and wean more pounds of calf over their lifetime.
items.post_text:
Cows that get pregnant early in the breeding season stay in the herd longer and wean heavier calves every year.

Kacie McCarthy, a beef cow-calf specialist at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, writes about it in Progressive Cattle this week. Pregnancy can be confirmed by rectal palpation, ultrasound, or blood test as early as 28 to 45 days after breeding, and the same check estimates fetal age and calving date.

That timing beats a simple open-or-bred answer. McCarthy cites research showing cows that conceive early stay in the herd longer and keep calving early in later years. Their calves come older and heavier at weaning, adding up to more pounds weaned over a cow's whole life. Late-bred cows often slip out of the calving window and leave the herd sooner. Daughters of early-breeding, good-weaning cows make the strongest replacement candidates, she writes.

A pregnancy test used to answer one question: in or out. Now it predicts which cows are worth keeping years from now.

Would a conception date change which cow you cull first this fall?

#reproduction #beefcattle #cowherdmanagement #cattlebreeding #agritech
items.author: Kacie McCarthy

items.headline: Using fresh cow data to target reproductive management decisions
items.summary: Tony Bruinje (South Dakota State University) writes that fresh cow health records and early heat activity during the voluntary waiting period can sort cows by reproductive potential; in a 17,000-cow study, cows with reproductive tract disease resumed cyclicity only 64-68% of the time versus 75-84% for healthy cows, and a Florida trial using targeted protocols instead of blanket synchronization added $108 gross profit per cow with fewer hormone treatments.
items.post_text:
Matching a cow's breeding protocol to her own heat activity data added $108 in profit per cow over blanket synchronization.

Tony Bruinje writes in Progressive Dairy this week. He is an assistant professor at South Dakota State University.

More than 40% of fresh cows carry a health issue before breeding. In one 17,000-cow study, those cows resumed normal cycling only 64% to 68% of the time. Healthy herdmates resumed it 75% to 84% of the time.

Activity monitors catch that gap early. Cows showing heat activity soon after calving were three times more likely to be detected in heat later. They were also twice as likely to be pregnant by 150 days in milk.

A Florida trial split cows this way. The active group got heat detection first. The rest went straight into a hormone-based sync protocol. Against syncing every cow the same way, it added $108 more profit per cow.

The data most farms already collect can hold the protocol decision.

Would sorting cows by their own signals change how your herd gets bred?

#reproduction #dairyfarming #cattlebreeding #precisionlivestock #dairygenetics

items.headline: Exclusive: Ayana Bio acquires Meati Foods assets for a steal to scale plant cell culture tech with Zenfold in India
items.summary: Boston plant cell culture startup Ayana Bio and India's Zenfold Sustainable Technologies jointly bought fermentation equipment from defunct alt-protein firm Meati Foods for $75,000: twelve 25,000-liter fermenters and seed trains, 300,000 liters of capacity, relocating to Zenfold's India site with a target of running by early 2027.
items.post_text:
Ayana Bio and an Indian partner picked up $75,000 of biomanufacturing gear that would cost millions to build new.

Elaine Watson, writing in AgFunderNews this week, reports the deal. Ayana Bio, a Boston plant cell culture startup, and Zenfold Sustainable Technologies in India jointly bought fermentation equipment from Meati Foods, the mycelium meat-alternative company that shut its Colorado plant in 2025.

The purchase: twelve 25,000-liter fermenters and their seed trains, 300,000 liters of capacity total, built at a facility Meati "spared no expense" on. Most of it sat unsold after a spring 2026 auction.

The tanks now move to Zenfold's site in India, aiming to run by early 2027. CEO Frank Jaksch called stainless steel cost a long-standing bottleneck for synthetic biology. He says the deal "fundamentally rewrites" Ayana's ability to scale plant cell lines like rosmarinic acid and saffron-derived crocins.

One company's shutdown became another's shortcut past years of fundraising and construction.

Would you rather build new capacity, or buy someone else's stranded assets?

#agritechdeals #biomanufacturing #startups #agtech #syntheticbiology
items.author: Elaine Watson

items.headline: Robigo Bio eyes commercialization for its ag biologicals with Leaps by Bayer investment
items.summary: Robigo Bio closed a Series A led by Leaps by Bayer (with Illumina Ventures, SVG Thrive, Congruent Ventures, Endeavor8) for engineered-microbe crop biologicals; its soybean Sudden Death Syndrome seed treatment tracks synthetic-chemistry performance at half the cost against a disease causing $200-500M in annual US losses, and its fusarium wilt product tripled yield versus untreated controls in trials.
items.post_text:
Robigo Bio says its engineered microbes can match crop chemistry performance at half the cost.

Jennifer Marston, writing in AgFunderNews this week, covers the Series A behind that claim. Leaps by Bayer led the round for Robigo Bio, a Cambridge, Massachusetts biologicals startup. Illumina Ventures, SVG Thrive, Congruent Ventures and Endeavor8 joined. Terms were not disclosed.

Robigo skips the usual route, screening wild microbes for useful traits. It picks organisms for shelf life and manufacturing cost, then engineers in the active ingredients. Founder Andee Wallace says the platform reaches field trial in under 20 months, against an industry norm of three to five years.

Early results back the pitch. A soybean seed treatment for Sudden Death Syndrome, a disease costing US growers $200 to $500 million a year, is tracking chemistry performance at half the price. A second product raised yields threefold against untreated fusarium wilt.

Biology usually loses to synthetic chemistry on cost. This pitch flips that math.

Would growers switch to a biological that only wins on price?

#agritechdeals #agbiologicals #cropprotection #agtech #startups
items.author: Jennifer Marston

items.headline: The behavior of the dairy cow: What motivates her drive in automated milking systems
items.summary: Lely's Dan Meihak explains that automated milking systems depend on voluntary cow visits, not a forced schedule; the industry standard underfeeds cows by 15 pounds of milk's worth at the bunk to drive robot visits, while herd dominance hierarchy and lameness govern who actually gets there and when.
items.post_text:
The industry standard for robotic dairies is to feed cows 15 pounds less milk's worth at the bunk than the herd actually produces.

Dan Meihak, a commercial product specialist at Lely North America, writes about it in Progressive Dairy this week. Automated milking only works if cows choose to walk to the robot. Nobody moves them on a schedule.

The lever is hunger. The feed bunk ration is engineered to leave an energy gap, closed only by the concentrated feed inside the robot stall. Landmark 2014 research found that lowering that ration's energy density raises voluntary visits. Feed the bunk too generously, and a cow has no reason to leave it.

Hunger alone will not guarantee a visit. Dominant, older cows control access and push heifers toward the robot during the night's quiet hours. Lameness is the single biggest disruptor: a cow in pain will skip her own feed reward rather than cross a concrete floor.

The robot only measures what the cow decides to do.

What in your barn is deciding it for her?

#dairyfarming #automatedmilking #precisionlivestock #cattlebehavior #dairytech
items.author: Dan Meihak

items.headline: xFarm Technologies’ acquisition of Sibium Analytics brings it closer to defining agriculture’s data layer
items.summary: xFarm Technologies acquired Brazil's Sibium Analytics, adding 8 million hectares of sugarcane monitoring to a platform that already covers 24 million hectares for over 600,000 farmers; the deal is xFarm's sixth acquisition in four years and pulls in ESG-audit and traceability tools ahead of 2027 biofuel documentation rules.
items.post_text:
xFarm just bought Sibium Analytics, extending its farm data platform into Brazil's sugarcane and biofuel supply chain.

AgFunderNews reported the deal this week. Sibium tracks 8 million hectares for nine of Brazil's largest sugarcane producers and built tools for crop monitoring, ESG audits and analytics. xFarm plans to roll those out across its own client base in Brazil and Europe.

The scale is what stands out. xFarm already serves over 600,000 farmers and manages 24 million hectares. This is its sixth acquisition in four years and second in Brazil alone. Brazil grows roughly half the world's sugarcane and exports it to 145 countries. About 80 percent of the country's ethanol comes from that crop, and new documentation rules land in 2027, exactly the gap Sibium's platforms were built to close.

Deals like this show where agtech money is heading: not new sensors, but full traceability from planting to buyer.

When does that infrastructure stop being a differentiator and start being the entry price?

#agritech #agtech #dataagriculture #sugarcane #mergersandacquisitions

items.headline: Where does the profit come from in automated milking?
items.summary: Alvaro Garcia cites a new Journal of Dairy Science study of Wisconsin dairies on guided-flow automated milking: cows averaging three milkings a day in their first 21 days after calving produced about 6 more pounds of milk daily through 150 days in milk, worth roughly $172 more revenue per cow at average US prices, though the study measured revenue rather than profit.
items.post_text:
Getting fresh cows to three milkings a day in their first 21 days added $172 in revenue per cow, a Wisconsin study found.

Alvaro Garcia writes about it in Progressive Dairy this week. He cites a new Journal of Dairy Science study of Wisconsin dairies on guided-flow automated milking.

Researchers compared cows averaging three milkings a day in their first three weeks after calving with cows that did not. The early group made about 6 more pounds of milk daily between 22 and 150 days in milk. That is 5.4% more milk revenue at average prices, about $172 per cow over the study. Those cows also carried higher butterfat and protein and lower somatic cell counts.

Each extra milking added less than the last, so gains shrink as frequency climbs. The study measured revenue, not profit. More milk still costs more feed, water and electricity.

A robot report showing three milkings a day by day 21 says nothing about whether the ration supports that output.

Does your feeding program get checked as often as your milking frequency numbers do?

#dairyfarming #automatedmilking #precisionlivestock #dairyeconomics
items.author: Alvaro Garcia

items.headline: Five Roads to Madison: The Cows, Families and Decisions Behind Five Elite Programs
items.summary: Bullvine profile of five elite Holstein breeding programs (Blondin, Jacobs, Boulet, Kueffner and Packard, Budjon) ahead of the 2026 World Dairy Expo Holstein show, judging each by whether its cows kept transmitting through daughters and sons rather than by show wins alone.
items.post_text:
The real test of a Holstein breeding program isn't the champion banner. It's whether the cow bred another one.

Andrew Hunt, writing in The Bullvine this week, traces that test through five programs ahead of World Dairy Expo's Holstein show on October 2. Ferme Jacobs swept the 2018 International Holstein Show with Loana EX-96-2E, then watched stablemate Aimo EX-95 beat her a month later at the Royal, the first Grand-and-Reserve sweep by homebred entries there since 1969.

Pierre Boulet built his Pierstein herd on the animal first, pedigree second, and has bred more than 200 Excellent cows since 1993. He also recalled paying $40,000 for a cow that never produced a single embryo. Budjon Farms became the first US breeder to sweep Grand Champion, Best Bred and Owned and Best Udder at three national shows in one year, 2005.

A champion photo lasts a season. A breeding system either keeps producing or it doesn't.

Which matters more when picking your next herd sire: the banner, or what came after it?

#dairygenetics #Holstein #cattlebreeding #WorldDairyExpo #pedigree
